tip.title: Who is it for?
tip.body:
The preposition **für** (for) always takes the accusative case. With a masculine noun, **der** becomes **den** and **ein** becomes **einen**.

The feminine, neuter, and plural articles keep the same form in the accusative. You can say **für das Einzelzimmer** or **für den Vater**.

examples.target: Der Schlüssel ist für das Doppelzimmer.
examples.source: The key is for the double room.

tip.title: Where are you heading?
tip.body:
When you want to know the destination, use **wohin** (where to). Compare it with **wo** (where), which asks for a fixed location.

Use **hin** for a journey there, and **zurück** for the journey back.

units.title: An invitation

tip.title: Adding some flavor
tip.body:
The word **denn** often doesn't translate directly. In questions, it makes you sound friendlier or more curious, a bit like "so" or "tell me" in English.

Separable verbs like **einladen** split in simple sentences. The **ein** goes right to the end!

sourceAccept: We are partying on the weekend.

sourceAccept: The party is at the weekend.

tip.title: Capitalizing on nouns
tip.body:
In German, every single noun starts with a capital letter. Not just names like Leon, but words like **Vorname** (first name) and **Land** (country).

This makes it very easy to spot the important words when you're filling out a form or reading a message!

sourceAccept: The message is intended for Leon.

tip.title: First this, then that
tip.body:
When you put a time word like **zuerst** (first) or **dann** (then) at the start of your sentence, the finite verb must stay in position two.

In these basic sentences, the subject therefore comes after the verb: **Zuerst kaufe ich ...**

sourceAccept: First, I am buying the ticket.
Then we are traveling to Berlin.
At last, we are in Berlin!
At last we are in Berlin!
